title: TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8 (atlasum.net)
comments: > TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8I know it's customary for HN to edit titles to remove extraneous information, but removing "Linux" here really takes away something useful and relevant.  This is a Linux vulnerability.  If you're running *BSD or Mac or Windows, not affected.reply

Quite, however it looks quite rare:"Why it's urgent: the bug sits in code every Linux server runs when it accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, before any application sees the connection. Anthropic, whose researcher reported it, says its Claude model wrote a working proof-of-concept exploit that runs commands as root on "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener," with no credentials. Go programs open those listeners by default, per the Go Security Team. See the timeline."I don't know of any Linux boxes running a multipath TCP listener in my care and I have quite a few.  MP generally implies a router of some sort and the intersections in a Venn diagram continue to get smaller ...This is still an issue and must be patched but I think it will be rare, very rare.reply

This is not rare. Every TCP connection in Go by default enables MPTCP [1]. Simply running a Go program that uses TCP without explicitly disabling this behavior will cause the running kernel to be vulnerable.1: https://groups.google.com/g/golang-announce/c/PCoQcdxoScwreply

to check. If you're running any Go code, you may be surprised. I was.reply

title: It's the memory latency, stupid (pivotlake.io)
comments: I work with another team at work that uses lots of message passing, C++ virtual methods in deeply nested class hierarchies, large DOMs and off-the-shelf C++ STL containers... on a STM32MP1, which has an in-order Cortex-A7 and a pittance of cache.On the other hand, in my team I wrote my custom C++ STL containers that allocate inline, SAX-style processing libraries and an object pool with links that use index+generations like 2000s video games... on a STM32H5 with less than a megabyte of RAM.Mechanical sympathy feels like a lost art to people I demonstrate it to... and I had to demonstrate to the first team with benchmark numbers that I would not be the bottleneck between us by orders of magnitudes.reply

I’ve had code review pushback against reorganizing data structures to be more cache-friendly on the grounds that it was “premature optimization” even though I pre-emotively justified the decision with benchmark results indicating that the performance difference was large and business relevant, and addressed a real performance bottleneck that I observed during testing.This was on a team and at a time where Clean Code was very popular. I somewhat wonder if the problem is that, in the 2010s, many people became convinced that certain aesthetic standards were both objectively, provably correct, and more important than anything else.reply

A lot of my poor opinion on developer opinions dates back to a couple projects where Product and Marketing were begging us for substantial performance improvements and the teams pushed back saying this was as fast as you could expect. I got 2x in the first six months on both projects, and delivered 25% per quarter on one for almost 2 years (that maths to around 8x) before I started to scrape the bottom of my barrel.It’s predominantly a way to shut down thinking, which is why it’s so often misquoted. Knuth’s version is more nuanced. Theirs is not at all.As a compromise I got really good at doing optimizations that also improved readability. Things like hoisting and better variable naming combined together can be mistaken for just code cleanup.I also discovered that keyhole optimizations are more palatable. Which is to say, move the slow bit yo a separate function with a single responsibility. Then do the optimization in a separate commit. Then the other devs don’t have to look at your changes and if they turn out to have a bug, we can always revert the change later. title: Zinc creep in cable spelter sockets brought down the Arecibo telescope in 2020 (maketecheasier.com)
comments: The forensic report on the failure of the cable sockets is at https://www.thorntontomasetti.com/sites/default/files/2022-0.... Unlike the linked article this includes detailed diagrams and discussion explaining how these sockets worked and how they failed.My attempt at a quick summary: the Arecibo instruments were held up by heavy steel cables, which are composed of a bundle of 126 to 216 individual wire strands twisted together, where each wire strand is about 1/4 inch diameter. At the cable ends these were anchored in sockets. The socket is conical, widening out towards where the wire ends go. The wire strands of the cable would be separated in a "broom" shape to fill out that conical area, and then the whole thing filled in with molten zinc.The failure mode of these zinc-filled sockets is for an inner core cylinder, about the same diameter as the cable body, to pull out from the socket while outer strands of the cable which are broomed out of that core either snap or pull free from the zinc plug.This failure mode hadn't really been seen prior to the Arecibo collapse, partly because it is a long term process where the zinc slowly flows under stress over decades.reply

title: Jepsen: ParticleDB 1.1.4 (jepsen.io)
comments: Brutal!> ParticleDB 1.1.4 claimed to be a Postgres-compatible database ... Instead, we found a library of confusion> exhibited frequent, profound transactional anomalies in essentially every way we could measure. We routinely observed the loss of committed writes, internal consistency violations, G1a (Aborted Read), G1b (Intermediate Read), and P4 (Lost Update). In the append workload, successfully appended values would routinely disappear from later reads of a given key. Our test suite inferred every kind of cyclic anomaly including G0, G1c, G-Single, and G2-item, but many of these can be attributed to more basic issues, like write loss. These issues occurred with a single server and without faults, and affected every transaction mode, interface, and WAL mode testedreply

I'm part of the ParticleDB team. We took these findings seriously and have spent the past few months addressing them and strengthening our testing. We now run sustained Jepsen workloads daily alongside our own test suites. We've also narrowed the supported transaction modes to focus development and testing on core correctness.Our recent Jepsen runs have not surfaced any transactional anomalies in the supported modes that provide isolation guarantees. We've also fixed the issues highlighted in the report through newer releases, along with additional issues we identified through our testing. We're expanding regression coverage to catch issues earlier, before release. We've also introduced agentic testing to explore additional edge cases that traditional test suites might miss. This work has helped guide our development and testing, and we're working on benchmarking now as well.reply

However, that same test harness failed immediately when run against ParticleDB 1.1.4. Orkes also stated they tested ParticleDB with SQLancer, which generates far more complex queries than the ones we tested. It is therefore perplexing that nearly every feature we tested exhibited glaring errors, and that our findings seemed to come as a surprise.Most databases have a test suite which exercises at least basic examples of each feature, and it is customary to run those tests before release, if not continuously. Where were those tests for ParticleDB? How does one add support for NOT NULL constraints without a test which tries to insert at least one NULL value? What development process adds a CHARACTER(10) type without trying to write a string of (e.g.) five characters?Our findings suggest structural deficiencies in the ParticleDB QA process. first_paragraph:
ParticleDB is a multi-model
    database designed for AI workloads. We tested versions 1.1.4 through
    1.1.18.11.rc-22 and found that ParticleDB’s claims of “Full ACID”
    were somewhat premature. We present 96 issues in ParticleDB, ranging
    from the pedestrian (crashes, deadlocks, data loss, etc.) to the
    piquant (partially-invisible rows which could not be deleted,
    WHERE 4 = 5, dropped tables re-emerging in distorted
    forms, confused columns, strings turning into integers, and so on).
    Most issues required just a single server, single client, and no
    faults. By version 1.1.18.11.rc-22, all but ten of those issues
    appeared resolved. However, ParticleDB continued to lose committed

When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session.We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server.
